newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bomb hits Paris Mosque, hurts one.
newsitem.headline: Bomb hits Paris Mosque, hurts one.

text.p: A crude bomb exploded at a Paris Mosque early on Monday, damaging the entrance and slightly injuring the caretaker of the building, police said.

No one immediately claimed responsibility for the explosion at 4.30 a.m. (0330 GMT), which also shattered windows of nearby buildings along the Rue de Tanger in a district of northeastern Paris that has many immigrant residents. Police sealed off the area.
The wounded man, the concierge of the Adda'Wa Mosque, was taken to hospital with hand njuries. "He is not seriously hurt," a police officer said.
Police said the bomb was placed at the entrance of the building, apparently in a fire-extinguisher stuffed with gunpowder with a slow fuse. It wrecked the door and damaged the entrance.
"We have no clues yet to guide the inquiry," a police officer said.
The head of the Mosque was known as a liberal who had good ties with other religions and with the local community.

The only recent controversy over the Mosque was a plan to build an extension to the building. The extreme right-wing National Front party had organised several demonstrations against the project in recent months.

A bomb last December planted by suspected Algerian Moslem extremists killed four people in an underground train in Paris. Algerian guerrillas accuse France of backing the military authorities in a war against them.

Algerian Islamic militants claimed responsibility for a previous bombing wave in 1995 which killed eight people and injured almost 200. Last December's bomb, and many of those in 1995, were explosives packed into hollowed-out gas canisters.
The 1995 wave of bombings was heralded by the shooting dead of a Moslem cleric, Sheikh Abdel-Baki Sahraoui, in another of the city's Mosques.
Security has been tight in Paris since the bombs, by Algeria's Armed Islamic Group (GIA), with troops guarding railway stations and airports.

Corsican separatists have set off thousands of small bombs on the Mediterranean island as part of a two-decade-long campaign for greater autonomy from France. But they rarely bomb on the mainland, do not choose religious targets and usually seek to avoid casualties.
Last week a small bomb exploded in a home decoration store in Paris, injuring one person in an attack that police said had no links to guerrilla violence.
